comment.value: This paper introduces the GreenHyperSpectra, a comprehensive multi-source hyperspectral dataset designed for vegetation trait prediction. It is a large and diverse dataset that includes real-world cross-sensor and cross-ecosystem samples, demonstrating robust generalization across different domains and sensors. The concerns raised by the reviewers, particularly regarding ground truth alignment uncertainty and the analysis of generalization, have been addressed. After carefully considering the comments and the rebuttal provided during the review period, I decided to accept the paper due to the significant contribution of the multi-source dataset and the advances in spectral representation learning for trait prediction.

author_final_remarks.value:
We thank the reviewers for their helpful feedback and engagement with our work, *"GreenHyperSpectra: A multi-source hyperspectral
dataset for global vegetation trait prediction."*  We appreciate the reviewers' recognition that our work "fill[s] a gap in existing datasets and provid[es] a valuable resource", shows "Strong generalization to new domains and sensors", and "opens a clear path for training large-scale foundation models". 

During the discussion period, in response to reviewers’ suggestions, we added several clarifications and improvements:

**Generalization analysis**: We clarified our cross-site, cross-sensor out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, where entire regions and acquisition setups are held out during testing, so as to simulate real-world deployment. We also added a vegetation-type-specific OOD analysis to assess model sensitivity when certain vegetation types are excluded from the test set.

**Noise robustness evaluation**: To assess model resilience to sensor-level distortions and environmental variability (e.g., illumination changes, calibration noise, or signal-to-noise ratio differences), we introduced additive Gaussian noise at inference time (σ = 0.01, 0.03, 0.05). MAE-based methods remained comparatively stable, reinforcing their utility for real-world applications.

**Improved presentation**: To enhance readability, we compiled a comprehensive table indexing all figures and tables across the manuscript and supplementary materials. We will include internal hyperlinks in the final version to facilitate easier navigation.
We also corrected a minor issue in the OOD evaluation for the MAE-FR-FT method. The main conclusion remains unchanged: MAE-FR-FT consistently outperforms all methods across most traits.

To conclude, we would like to highlight our main contributions:
- We present GreenHyperSpectra, a multi-source hyperspectral dataset for vegetation trait prediction covering diverse sensors, ecosystems, and acquisition conditions—substantially expanding resources for spectral representation learning.
- We introduce and benchmark semi- and self-supervised methods for 1D hyperspectral regression of multiple plant traits.
- We demonstrate strong performance gains over fully supervised baselines, particularly in low-label and cross-datasets (OOD) settings and under varying sensor configurations.
- We offer reproducible benchmarks and rigorous evaluations to support future research in hyperspectral trait estimation.

We would like to thank the Reviewer for their feedback and comments. We greatly appreciate the time and effort invested in reviewing our manuscript. We respond to specific comments and questions below.

**1- The reported linear-probe accuracies are markedly lower than fine-tuned ones (Tables 2-4), yet no contrastive methods (e.g., SimCLR-style spectral encoders) are included. Linear probing is a stronger litmus test of representation quality; adding contrastive pre-training and reporting its linear-probe scores would strengthen claims.**

We thank the Reviewer for this good suggestion. Regarding contrastive methods such as SimCLR, we note that designing physically meaningful and semantically faithful augmentations for hyperspectral data is quite challenging. This issue has been explicitly raised in [103], which highlights that most existing augmentations used in contrastive learning (e.g., spectral mirroring, color distortions) are not physically grounded and may distort key semantic traits in hyperspectral signals. Such distortions are especially problematic in our setting, where biochemical traits are tightly linked to subtle spectral variations. For this reason, we concentrated on masked spectral reconstruction via MAE, which avoids relying on ill-defined augmentations and instead encourages the model to learn robust intra-spectral correlations. We believe this is more aligned with the physical structure of hyperspectral data and more appropriate for trait prediction.

To complement this analysis, we have responded to the Reviewer’s comment by implementing a simple SimCLR-style architecture using Gaussian noise spectral augmentations. The resulting linear probe performance was indeed lower than our masked reconstruction approach (see Table 2), supporting our concern that current augmentations used for contrastive setups are not well-suited to hyperspectral trait learning tasks.

**2- Fig. 5 shows limited performance gains when the labeled fraction rises from 20 % to 100 %. The paper should explain why extra supervision saturates so early—e.g., label noise, model capacity limits, or redundancy in the trait space.**

Thanks for catching the typo in the x axis!

We would like to clarify that Fig. 5 analyzes the effect of increasing the **unlabeled data** fraction used during pretraining, not the labeled supervision fraction. As noted in Lines 295–298, we hypothesize that our stratified sampling protocol, which ensures balanced representation across sensors, ecosystems, and acquisition conditions within all splits, allows the model to learn rich, generalizable features even from relatively small subsets of unlabeled data with high variability. We will make this clearer in the revised draft.
That being said, we note that MAE_FT reached best performance with 60% of the unlabeled set, and RTM-AE with 80% of the the unlabeled set, including specific trait trends, showing that we still increase performance by using a significant portion of the unlabeled dataset in the context of the study presented in Figure 5.

**Erratum: Correction to MAE-FR-FT OOD Evaluation**

We identified and corrected an implementation issue affecting the OOD evaluation of the MAE-FR-FT model reported in Table 4 of the original submission. The updated results will be reflected in the camera ready version of the manuscript. As expected, performance metrics for MAE-FR-FT are now more conservative than initially reported: R² dropped from 0.757(±0.041) to 0.311(±0.076) on average. It aligns better with the general behavior of all models under real-world distribution shifts. Importantly, this correction does not change the main conclusion: MAE-FR-FT remains the top-performing method on average, outperforming all baselines across most traits.


We thank the Reviewer for their time and consideration. We appreciate the pre-rebuttal Borderline Accept score. As in our experience, the Datasets and Benchmarks Track has had a higher threshold for acceptance than Main Track, we would appreciate your considering raising your score to Accept if you feel our responses have largely addressed your concerns.

We would like to thank the Reviewer for their feedback and comments. We greatly appreciate the time and effort invested in reviewing our manuscript. We respond to specific comments and questions below.

**1- Ground truth alignment uncertainty: The USDA CDL is coarse and can introduce label noise when overlaid on fine-resolution data.**

We would like to clarify that coarse USDA CDL labels are not used at any stage in our dataset pipeline - neither during pretraining nor as supervision targets. The trait data we use was either measured directly in field plots or assigned using community-weighted means (CWMs) at the pixel level, based on ground-measured species composition. This ensures alignment at the appropriate spatial resolution and avoids label noise from coarse land cover overlays. We will make these points clearer in the text.

**2- Insufficient spectral ablation analysis: It remains unclear which spectral bands or resolutions contribute most to model gains.**

We thank the Reviewer for this valuable feedback. In response to this suggestion, we conducted an additional analysis of feature attribution of the MAE model, illustrating which bands contribute most across different traits. We considered three use cases: MAE finetuned with linear probing, MAE finetuned at a specific block, and MAE fully finetuned. For each model, we illustrate the gradient amplitude for each trait with respect to each individual spectral dimension. This shows the impact of each spectral feature within the prediction of each trait. Interestingly, we note that the more the MAE is finetuned, the lower the variance of the gradients and the more precise the impact of each spectral feature. Unfortunately we can not provide this visual analysis in the rebuttal since images and links are not permitted, but will include it in the camera ready version as it helps to demonstrate the model’s internal spectral attention and supports its physical plausibility.
Overall, hyperspectral data has been shown to be highly valuable for accurately estimating plant traits such as chlorophyll, water content, and leaf mass per area [137–140]. Moreover, trait-specific sensitivity varies across the spectrum: chlorophyll absorption features dominate the visible range, while traits like water content and leaf mass per area are more strongly expressed in the SWIR region.

[137] Bach, H., & Mauser, W. (1997, January). Improvements of plant parameter estimations with hyperspectral data compared to multispectral data. In Remote Sensing of Vegetation and Sea (Vol. 2959, pp. 59-67). SPIE.

[138] Homolová, L., Malenovský, Z., Clevers, J. G., García-Santos, G., & Schaepman, M. E. (2013). Review of optical-based remote sensing for plant trait mapping. Ecological Complexity, 15, 1-16.

[139] Shiklomanov, A. N., Dietze, M. C., Viskari, T., Townsend, P. A., & Serbin, S. P. (2016). Quantifying the influences of spectral resolution on uncertainty in leaf trait estimates through a Bayesian approach to RTM inversion. Remote Sensing of Environment, 183, 226-238.

[140] Zhou, J., Wang, B., Fan, J., Ma, Y., Wang, Y., & Zhang, Z. (2022). A systematic study of estimating potato N concentrations using UAV-based hyper-and multi-spectral imagery. Agronomy, 12(10), 2533.

**3- Generalization scope is not deeply analyzed: Models are evaluated mostly in-region, without extensive cross-region generalization testing.**

We would like to clarify that our out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation protocol is specifically designed to assess generalization across regions and acquisition conditions, which represent key dimensions of real-world variability in remote sensing applications.
In our OOD setting (see Section 5, Lines 256-266), we adopt a cross-site evaluation protocol. The labelled dataset includes 50 distinct acquisitions (each representing a different site and different experiment), which we divide into 10 non-overlapping groups, each containing 5 sites. In each fold, one group (i.e., 5 unseen sites) is held out entirely for testing, while the remaining 45 sites are used for training. This process is repeated so that every site is used for testing exactly once. This strategy ensures that the model is evaluated on entirely unseen regions with different ecological, temporal, and sensor conditions, representing a realistic and rigorous test of generalization compared to conventional random splits (within-region validation).

**4- Lack of temporal consistency: The AVIRIS-NG and PlanetScope data are not temporally synchronized, limiting analysis of phenology or seasonal trends.**

We would like to clarify that PlanetScope is not part of our dataset. While we included multi-temporal acquisitions to increase ecological diversity and model robustness, we acknowledge that synchronized time-series analysis is currently limited by two factors:
  (1) The lack of open-source, time-synchronized hyperspectral datasets spanning the same regions.
  (2) The relatively recent deployment of spaceborne hyperspectral missions, which still lack dense temporal coverage.
As a result, this limits the feasibility of seasonally synchronized time series analysis across sensors. 

**Erratum: Correction to MAE-FR-FT OOD Evaluation** 

We identified and corrected an implementation issue affecting the OOD evaluation of the MAE-FR-FT model reported in Table 4 of the original submission. The updated results will be reflected in the camera ready version of the manuscript. As expected, performance metrics for MAE-FR-FT are now more conservative than initially reported: R² dropped from 0.757(±0.041) to 0.311(±0.076) on average. These results align better with the general behavior of all models under real-world distribution shifts. Importantly, this correction does not change the main conclusion: MAE-FR-FT remains the top-performing method on average, outperforming all baselines across most traits.

We would like to thank the Reviewer for their feedback and comments. We greatly appreciate the time and effort invested in reviewing our manuscript. We respond to specific comments and questions below.

**1- The paper empirically demonstrates MAE’s superiority but lacks theoretical justification (e.g., why masked spectral reconstruction improves trait generalizability).**

We thank the Reviewer for pointing this out. While our focus was empirical, we agree that additional justification strengthens the contribution. MAE enables the model to learn localized correlations and long-range dependencies within hyperspectral signals, by reconstructing both across adjacent tokens and distant tokens. In our setting, each token represents 20 contiguous bands, allowing the model to capture fine-grained correlations. These correlations reflect underlying biochemical traits, such as how chlorophyll absorption in visible bands and water content in SWIR jointly affect spectral shape. Many traits are not associated with single-band features but instead depend on combinations of multiple regions of the spectrum (e.g., LAI relates to both chlorophyll and NIR plateau shape; see [64, 135, 136, 141]). The pretext task of MAE forces the model to learn such relationships without explicit supervision, providing a strong prior on trait-relevant structure. This prior enables better generalization and more efficient fine-tuning in downstream regression tasks, as empirically shown in our experiments.

[64] S. Jacquemoud and S. Ustin. Leaf optical properties. Cambridge University Press, 2019

[135] Ollinger, S. V. (2011). Sources of variability in canopy reflectance and the convergent properties of plants. New Phytologist, 189(2), 375-394.

[136] Serbin, S. P., & Townsend, P. A. (2020). Scaling functional traits from leaves to canopies. In Remote sensing of plant biodiversity (pp. 43-82). Cham: Springer International Publishing.

[141] Kumar, L., Schmidt, K., Dury, S., & Skidmore, A. (2002). Imaging spectrometry and vegetation science. In Imaging spectrometry: basic principles and prospective applications (pp. 111-155). Dordrecht: Springer Netherlands.

**2- Class imbalance (Fig. 7): Underrepresented biomes (e.g., tropical rainforests) may skew OOD results.**

This is an excellent question. We first wish to clarify that in general, existing labeled datasets do not cover all biomes evenly - as illustrated in Figure 2. To address this, we explicitly included diverse biomes in our pretraining set, which we believe enhances representation learning and benefits downstream applications.
In response to the Reviewer’s suggestion, we have analyzed OOD performance by vegetation type, which confirms that while performance varies slightly across ecosystems, on average the gains of our fully finetuned model pretrained with MAE  (MAE_ FT) hold consistently.
Due to response length constraints, we present only the average results over the traits (the outputs). However, we will add the complete evaluation per individual trait to the supplemental materials of the camera ready version, and we can share them with the reviewer if needed.

We thank the Reviewer for this helpful observation. We agree that Figs. 12–15 in the Supplementary Materials contain redundant detail and partially duplicate results already presented in Tables 2 and 3 of the main manuscript. To improve clarity and focus, we will remove the two figures that do not provide additional insight (Figs. 14 and 15) and revise the remaining heatmaps to better highlight key trends, particularly the consistent performance gains of MAE fine-tuning (MAE-FR-FT) across both full-range and half-range inputs.
In the meantime, all underlying numerical results are available in the main manuscript to ensure transparency and reproducibility. We welcome any additional suggestions to further improve the presentation.

We thank the Reviewer for these observations. Regarding RTM-AE’s lower performance on Anth, a potential explanation is that Anth labels are available only for grassland-related observations, while RTM-AE’s correction block is optimized for generalization across multiple vegetation types. This may reduce specificity for traits concentrated in a single vegetation type. For cbc, we confirm this is a specific case: in RTM-AE, cbc is not directly predicted but is derived from cm and cp estimates (cm-cp), making it more sensitive to compound error from both components. We will clarify this in the camera ready version.

We agree that MAE-FR-LP, standing for MAE pretrained on full range and fine-tuned with linear probing, underperforms in OOD settings (Table 4). We attribute this to the limited flexibility of the frozen encoder, which retains only general and low-level spectral correlations and exposes very few trainable parameters due to the linear probing during downstream learning. As a result, it struggles to adapt to distribution shifts. This limitation was noted in the results discussion (see Line 324-326).

We identified and corrected an implementation issue affecting the OOD evaluation of the MAE-FR-FT model reported in Table 4 of the original submission. Importantly, this correction does not change the main conclusion: MAE-FR-FT remains the top-performing method on average, outperforming all baselines across most traits.

GreenHyperSpectra is a large, diverse hyperspectral dataset covering multiple sensors, ecosystems, and decades.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper empirically demonstrates MAE’s superiority but lacks theoretical justification (e.g., why masked spectral reconstruction improves trait generalizability).  

2. Class imbalance (Fig. 7): Underrepresented biomes (e.g., tropical rainforests) may skew OOD results.  

3. Sensor heterogeneity (Table 5): No quantitative analysis of how cross-sensor noise impacts performance. Experiments with synthetic noise (e.g., Gaussian sensor noise) should be added to test robustness.  

4. Overwhelming detail in Figs. 12-15 obscures key trends (e.g., MAE’s HR-to-FR transferability).  In addition, OOD metrics lack per-dataset breakdowns (e.g., which ecosystems degrade performance) in Table 4.  

5. RTM-AE underperforms on Anth (Table 2) and cbc (Fig. 16), but no root-cause analysis. In addition, MAE-FR-LP’s poor OOD performance (Table 4) is unexplained.  

6. The paper’s dataset and benchmarking are strong contributions, but theoretical depth, bias analysis, and clarity of results need improvement. Addressing these would strengthen its impact for NeurIPS.

Addressing challenges like label scarcity and domain shifts, the dataset spans multiple sensors and ecosystems. The authors propose an evaluation framework for in- and out-of-distribution trait prediction and show that pretraining on GreenHyperSpectra significantly improves label-efficient regression performance over supervised baselines.

Generalization scope is not deeply analyzed: Models are evaluated mostly in-region, without extensive cross-region generalization testing.
Lack of temporal consistency: The AVIRIS-NG and PlanetScope data are not temporally synchronized, limiting analysis of phenology or seasonal trends.

summary.value: The paper presents GreenHyperSpectra, a collection of >140 k vegetation canopy reflectance spectra acquired from proximal, airborne and satellite platforms spanning 1992-2024 and diverse biomes. The authors position the dataset as a large-scale pre-training resource for semi/self-supervised spectral representation learning aimed at leaf- and canopy-level trait regression. They benchmark three paradigms, against a state-of-the-art supervised CNN baseline on full-range (400–2450 nm), half-range (VNIR-only) and out-of-distribution (OOD) splits. MAE fine-tuning delivers the highest average $R^{2}$ gains and lowest nRMSE, demonstrating that large unlabeled spectral corpora substantially reduce label demands for global vegetation-trait mapping.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. GreenHyperSpectra opens a clear path for training large-scale foundation models that generalize to global vegetation-trait prediction tasks

2. The dataset aggregates spectra across three sensor classes and multiple continents, far surpassing single-sensor corpora like SpectralEarth.

3. The study compares supervised, self-supervised, and physics-guided approaches, including a PROSAIL-aware RTM-AE.

4. The manuscript is well-structured; diagrams (Fig. 1, Fig. 3) and tables are self-contained, and acronyms are defined early.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The reported linear-probe accuracies are markedly lower than fine-tuned ones (Tables 2-4), yet no contrastive methods (e.g., SimCLR-style spectral encoders) are included. Linear probing is a stronger litmus test of representation quality; adding contrastive pre-training and reporting its linear-probe scores would strengthen claims.

2. Fig. 5 shows limited performance gains when the labeled fraction rises from 20 % to 100 %. The paper should explain why extra supervision saturates so early—e.g., label noise, model capacity limits, or redundancy in the trait space.

title.value: GreenHyperSpectra: A multi-source hyperspectral dataset for global vegetation trait prediction

TLDR.value: Learning spectral representation from diverse hyperspectral data to improve plant trait prediction (multi-regression)

abstract.value:
Plant traits such as leaf carbon content and leaf mass are essential variables in the study of biodiversity and climate change. However, conventional field sampling cannot feasibly cover trait variation at ecologically meaningful spatial scales. 
Machine learning represents a valuable solution for plant trait prediction across ecosystems, leveraging hyperspectral data from remote sensing.
Nevertheless, trait prediction from hyperspectral data is challenged by label scarcity and substantial domain shifts (\eg across sensors, ecological distributions), requiring robust cross-domain methods.
Here, we present GreenHyperSpectra, a pretraining dataset encompassing real-world cross-sensor and cross-ecosystem samples designed to benchmark trait prediction with semi- and self-supervised methods. We adopt an evaluation framework encompassing in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. 
We successfully leverage GreenHyperSpectra to pretrain label-efficient multi-output regression models that outperform the state-of-the-art supervised baseline. 
Our empirical analyses demonstrate substantial improvements in learning spectral representations for trait prediction, establishing a comprehensive methodological framework to catalyze research at the intersection of representation learning and plant functional traits assessment. We also share the dataset\footnotemark[1], code and pretrained model objects for this study \href{https://github.com/echerif18/HyspectraSSL}{here}.

\footnotetext[1]{GreenHyperSpectra dataset: \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/Avatarr05/GreenHyperSpectra}{https://huggingface.co/datasets/Avatarr05/GreenHyperSpectra}}
